alt: Eye-tracking shows which parts of an advert are looked at and for how long; EEG records brain activity as an indication of attention and emotional engagement. Both give objective data, as in Ciceri et al. (2020), but show physiological reactions rather than liking or intention to buy.
caption: Objective measures of attention, but not of liking or buying.

alt: Four rows map each of the seller's 4 Ps to a consumer-side C: product to consumer wants and needs, price to cost, place to convenience, promotion to communication, each with the question the advertiser asks.
caption: Each P becomes a C when you take the customer's point of view.

alt: Definitions of high and low self-monitors, then a study card for Snyder and DeBono (1985) study 3: aim, procedure using the Self-Monitoring Scale and image or quality adverts, and results. A conclusion note and an evaluation grid covering application, self-reports, generalisation and determinism follow.
caption: Image appeals suit high self-monitors; quality claims suit low self-monitors.

alt: A two-by-two grid: high self-monitors pay more for a product with an image appeal, low self-monitors pay more for one with a quality claim. Applied to the watch example, the celebrity party advert goes to high self-monitors and the accuracy advert to low self-monitors.
caption: The finding is an interaction: neither appeal wins for everyone.

alt: Children watched either a Home Alone clip in which Pepsi appears or a control clip, then chose a cola. Those who saw the placement more often chose Pepsi, most of all if they had seen the film before. Two explanations follow: reminder and mere exposure.
caption: Placement nudged choice, most strongly as a reminder for children who knew the film.

alt: Study card for Fischer et al. (1991): children aged 3 to 6 matched logos to product pictures; recognition rose with age and many matched Old Joe the Camel to a cigarette. An application point and validity limits follow.
caption: Young children recognise brands before they understand what advertising is for.

alt: Brand awareness (recognising or recalling a brand) is contrasted with brand image (associations and feelings). Below, the four functions of slogans and Kohli et al.'s (2007) guidelines for effective slogans.
caption: Awareness is recognition; image is association. Slogans build both.
